a: one of the leaders of the Pharisees
p: The third time in Luke that Jesus eats at a Pharisee's table, and once again he is being watched.
b: Luke alone tells of Jesus dining with Pharisees, three times (7:36; 11:37; 14:1). The Pharisees had no official rulers; "one of the leaders" means a man of standing among them, perhaps a member of a town council or of the Sanhedrin, as Nicodemus was (John 3:1). The main Sabbath meal came at midday, after the synagogue service, and was cooked the day before, since no fire was kindled on the Sabbath (Exodus 16:23; 35:3). "Keeping a close eye on him" translates the verb Luke used when scribes and Pharisees watched to see whether he would heal on a Sabbath (6:7). Luke's Pharisees are not simple villains: they host Jesus, and some warn him of Herod (13:31).

t: Dropsy, and a picture of greed
p: Dropsy was a swelling with fluid. Ancient moralists used it as a picture of greed that can never drink enough.
b: The adjective ὑδρωπικός, used only here in the New Testament, names the swelling doctors now call edema, which often comes from failing heart, kidneys or liver. W. K. Hobart (1882) listed words like this to prove that Luke was a physician; H. J. Cadbury showed that educated writers who were not doctors used the same words, so the argument proves little. In Greek and Roman moral writing dropsy was a stock image of greed, because the sufferer is always thirsty though full of water (Horace, Odes 2.2). Willi Braun argued that Luke placed this healing at the head of a chapter about status-seeking and wealth for that reason.

t: Healing on the Sabbath: whose rule?
p: The Law forbade work on the Sabbath but never said whether healing was work. Jewish teachers disagreed.
b: The Ten Words forbid work on the seventh day (Exodus 20:10), but the Torah does not say whether healing counts as work. Teachers of Jesus' day argued the details. The Damascus Document, a rule book of a strict Jewish sect, forbids even lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (Damascus Document 11:13–14). The later rabbis held that saving a life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), but a long illness like dropsy could wait a day, as the synagogue leader says in 13:14. "Lawyers" (νομικοί) is Luke's usual word for the experts in the Law of Moses whom Mark and Matthew call scribes (7:30; 10:25; 11:45–52). This is Luke's fourth Sabbath healing (4:31–39; 6:6–11; 13:10–17).

t: An argument from what they already do
p: Jesus appeals to what his hearers would surely do for a son or an ox in trouble on the Sabbath.
b: Jesus does not cite a ruling. He points to what any of his hearers would do without thinking twice. The stricter view at Qumran forbade lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (Damascus Document 11:13–14), and the later rabbis allowed only indirect help to an animal, such as bringing cushions so it could climb out (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 128b). A son, though, would be pulled out at once. The pairing "a son, or an ox" is odd, and copyists changed it (see the variant), but it makes the point stronger: if you would rescue your child or your animal, why not this man? Compare the ox and donkey led to water in 13:15 and the sheep in Matthew 12:11.

p: Jesus' advice about seats retells Proverbs 25:6–7, and Luke calls it a parable.
b: At a formal meal guests reclined on couches, and the places nearest the host were the most honored (Matthew 23:6). Jesus' advice repeats an old proverb: "It is better for him to say to you, 'Come up here,' than for him to move you down in front of a noble" (Proverbs 25:7). Luke calls it a parable, because the Greek παραβολή, like Hebrew mashal, covers proverbs and sayings as well as stories. The words are more than table manners. The verb "choosing" and the saying in 14:11 show that Jesus is speaking of how God ranks people, and Luke's readers knew the later scene in which the disciples argue at table about who is greatest (22:24–27).

a: everyone who raises himself up will be brought low
p: The same saying closes the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14), and Matthew has it too.
b: This saying appears again word for word at 18:14 and in Matthew 23:12. The passive verbs, "will be brought low" and "will be raised up," leave God as the one who acts, a common Jewish way of speaking. It sums up one of Luke's main themes, already sung by Mary, who praised God for pulling down rulers and lifting up the lowly (1:52). The prophets used the same pattern (Ezekiel 21:26; compare Proverbs 29:23). At a dinner where guests jostle for honor, Jesus says that the only seat worth having is the one God gives.

a: They might invite you back in turn
p: In the Roman world a dinner was an investment: you fed people who could feed you back.
b: Meals in the ancient Mediterranean world were part of a system of exchange. Hosts invited equals or betters, expecting to be invited back, and patrons fed clients who repaid them with loyalty and praise. A dinner list showed and secured a family's rank. Jesus tells his host to step outside that system: invite people who can never return the favor. Joel Green and others note that this cuts against the way honor was earned in Luke's world, Jewish and Greek alike. The "repayment" Jesus promises comes from God (14:14), as in 6:32–35, where lending to those who cannot repay makes you "children of the Most High."

t: The guests the holy were keeping out
p: Jesus names the very people a Qumran rule barred from the end-time assembly and its meal.
b: The list matters. The Law kept a priest who was blind or lame from offering sacrifices: "no man who is blind or lame" (Leviticus 21:18). The Rule of the Congregation (1QSa) 2:3–9, a Qumran text about Israel in the last days, shut out of the assembly anyone who was lame, blind, deaf or marked with a visible blemish, because angels would be present; the same text then describes the meal with the Messiah. Jesus invites exactly these people, as he had announced good news to the poor and sight for the blind (4:18; 7:22). The guest list of 14:21 is the same four groups.
r: Leviticus 21:17–23; 2 Samuel 5:8; Rule of the Congregation 2:3–9; 4:18; 7:22; 14:21

a: at the resurrection of the righteous
p: A hope the Pharisee host shared: God will raise the righteous and reward them.
b: Pharisees believed in the resurrection of the dead, against the Sadducees (Acts 23:8), so Jesus speaks to his host in terms he accepts. "The resurrection of the righteous" goes back to Daniel 12:2, where many who sleep in the dust awake, some to everlasting life. Elsewhere Luke speaks of a resurrection "of the righteous and the unrighteous alike" (Acts 24:15); here only the reward is in view. The point is not to give in order to get a larger reward later, but to stop keeping score, and leave the paying back to God.

t: The feast at the end of the age
p: The guest pictures the kingdom as a banquet, as Isaiah did. Jesus' parable asks who will actually come.
b: Isaiah foresaw a feast God would spread "for all the peoples" (Isaiah 25:6), and Jesus spoke of many coming from east and west to "lie down to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 8:11; compare Luke 13:28–29). The guest's pious remark assumes that he and those like him will be at that table. The parable that follows answers him: the invited guests may refuse, and others will take their places. In the Byzantine text the guest says "dinner" rather than "bread" (see the variants).

a: he invited a lot of people
p: A host invited guests ahead of time, then sent a slave to call them when the food was ready.
b: A great dinner came with two invitations. Guests were invited in advance, and when the meal was ready a slave went to bring them. Esther invites the king and Haman to "the feast that I will make for them" (Esther 5:8), and on the day the king's eunuchs "rushed Haman off to the feast" (Esther 6:14). Those invited in this parable had already said yes. Turning down the second call at the last minute, after the animals were slaughtered and the food prepared, was a public insult to the host. Matthew's version of the story is about a king's wedding feast for his son and is more violent (Matthew 22:1–14); see the chapter page.

p: Readers disagree whether the excuses are honest reasons or thin pretexts that insult the host.
b: Kenneth Bailey argued, from his years in Middle Eastern villages, that every excuse is transparently false: no one buys a field without seeing it, or five pairs of oxen without testing them, and the evening meal does not stop a man from looking at his property. On this reading the guests are snubbing the host. Others read the excuses as ordinary, even reasonable business and family concerns, which is the danger: the good things of life crowd out God's call (8:14). The third excuse echoes the Law, which freed a newly married man from army service for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5; compare Deuteronomy 20:5–7), but a dinner is not a war.

a: Hurry out into the squares and lanes of the town
t: First the town, then the roads
p: Many readers see two missions here: first to Israel's outcasts, then beyond, to the Gentiles.
b: The master sends his slave twice. First he goes to the town's own poor and disabled, then out to the roads and hedgerows beyond the town (14:23). Many interpreters, from the church fathers to Joachim Jeremias, read this as an outline of the mission in Luke-Acts: Jesus' call to the outcasts within Israel (tax collectors and sinners, 15:1), then the apostles' turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46; 28:28). Others, such as Klyne Snodgrass, warn against reading allegory into every detail and take the second sending simply as the host's determination to fill his house.

t: "Compel them to come in": a verse with a long shadow
p: Augustine used this verse to defend forcing heretics back into the church. In the story it is urgent hospitality.
b: The verb ἀναγκάζω means to compel or to press hard. In the story it is the urgency of hospitality: strangers asked to a rich man's house would decline out of politeness, as Lot's guests did until "he pressed them hard" (Genesis 19:3), and as the Emmaus disciples urged Jesus to stay (24:29). The Latin compelle intrare, "compel them to come in," had a darker history. Augustine cited it to defend imperial laws forcing the Donatists, a breakaway African church, back into the Catholic Church (Letters 93 and 185). Medieval and early modern writers used it to justify persecution, and Pierre Bayle wrote a whole book against that use in 1686. See the chapter page.

p: "I tell you" is plural. The master turns to the table guests, and his voice merges with Jesus' own.
b: "I tell you" (λέγω ὑμῖν) is addressed to a plural "you," though the master has been speaking to one slave. The storyteller seems to step out of the story and speak to the dinner guests around Jesus. "My supper" then sounds like Jesus' own banquet, the kingdom feast of 14:15. Luke uses the same move elsewhere (11:8; 18:8). Some later manuscripts add, from Matthew 22:14, "For the called are many, but the chosen are few" (see the variant).
orig: λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν (legō gar hymin), 'for I tell you (plural)'

a: does not hate his father and mother
t: "Hate": a Hebrew way of saying "put second"
p: In Hebrew idiom, to "hate" one person and "love" another means to prefer the second. Matthew says "loves more."
b: Hebrew and Aramaic often set "love" and "hate" side by side to mean "prefer" and "put second." Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Genesis says Leah was "hated" (Hebrew senu'ah); the site renders it "The LORD saw that Leah was the unloved one" (Genesis 29:31). Compare the "loved" and "unloved" wives of Deuteronomy 21:15–17 and Malachi 1:2–3. Matthew gives the sense: "Someone who loves father or mother over me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:37). Still, Luke's word is stronger on purpose. In a world where family was everything, Jesus claims a loyalty above it, and Luke adds the wife and "his own life." The same Jesus commands honoring parents (18:20) and loving enemies (6:27).

a: carry his own cross and come behind me
p: Luke later shows Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross "behind Jesus", a picture of this saying.
b: A man condemned to crucifixion carried the crossbeam to the place of execution (John 19:17). Jesus has already said that whoever follows him must take up the cross "every day" (9:23). Here the verb is βαστάζω, "carry, bear," and "come behind me" repeats the words of 9:23. Luke later shows Simon of Cyrene made to carry the cross "behind Jesus" (23:26), the only person in the Gospels who literally carries a cross behind Jesus. Matthew has the same saying in his mission discourse (Matthew 10:38) and Mark in Mark 8:34.

p: A tower was a farm building or a watchtower over a vineyard. A half-finished one was a public joke.
b: A πύργος could be a watchtower in a vineyard, as in Isaiah's song (Isaiah 5:2) and Jesus' parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1), or a larger farm building. Stone was costly, and an abandoned foundation stood for years as a mark of a man's poor planning. In an honor culture the mockery of the neighbors was a real cost. The tower and the king's war (14:31–32) are twin parables, found only in Luke: both say, count the cost before you start. Some ask whether a disciple can ever have "enough" to finish; the answer of 14:33 is that he finishes by giving everything up.

a: marching out to clash with another king in battle
t: A lost war Luke's readers remembered?
p: Some scholars have suggested that Luke's readers thought of Herod Antipas, who went to war with King Aretas and lost. Others doubt it.
b: Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabataean king Aretas IV, to marry Herodias. Around AD 36 Aretas made war on him and destroyed his army, and Josephus reports that many Jews took the defeat as God's punishment for Antipas' killing of John the Baptist (Josephus, Antiquities 18.109–119). Some scholars have heard an echo of that war in this parable: a king who did not count the cost. The war came after Jesus' ministry, so it cannot lie behind his words, but Luke's readers, who knew the story of Antipas (3:19–20; 9:7–9; 13:31–32; 23:6–12), may have thought of it. Korinna Zamfir, surveying the proposal, judges the parallel far from obvious: the parable's weaker king sues for peace in time, which Antipas did not do. Nothing in the text requires the link.

a: say goodbye to all his possessions
p: The verb means "bid farewell" or "renounce". The early church used it at baptism: "I renounce you, Satan."
b: Ἀποτάσσομαι means to take leave of someone, as the would-be follower who wanted first "to say goodbye" to his family (9:61), and Paul taking leave of friends (Acts 18:18, 21). Here its object is a person's possessions: the disciple parts from them as from people left behind. In the baptism rites of the early church the candidate faced west and said, "I renounce you, Satan" (ἀποτάσσομαί σοι), with the same verb, as the Mystagogical Catecheses attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem explain to the newly baptized (1.4–5). Luke is the Gospel that presses hardest on possessions (5:11, 28; 12:33; 18:22), yet it also praises Zacchaeus, who gave half (19:8). How literally the saying binds every Christian is debated; see the card on Matthew 19:21.

p: The verb means "become foolish". Salt from the Dead Sea, mixed with other minerals, could lose its taste.
b: Luke uses the same verb as Matthew 5:13, μωραίνω, which usually means "to become foolish" (Romans 1:22). His question, "what will it be seasoned with?", is Mark's (Mark 9:50) put in the passive, though Mark says the salt becomes "unsalty" (ἄναλον). Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness, but the salt gathered around the Dead Sea was mixed with gypsum and other minerals, and when damp the salt could leach out, leaving a tasteless crust. Some scholars suggest a play on Aramaic words for "salty" and "foolish." In Luke the saying closes the call to count the cost: a disciple who will not pay it is like salt that has gone flat. See the note on Matthew 5:13.

a: no good for the land, and no good for the dung heap
t: Not even fit for the manure pile
p: Salt was used in small amounts on fields and in manure. Flat salt is not good even for that.
b: Ancient farmers used small amounts of salt on some soils and mixed it into dung heaps, and several commentators read the verse that way: salt that has lost its taste cannot even be used as fertilizer. Others think "for the land" and "for the dung heap" are just a vivid way of saying "good for nothing." Either way, the end is the same: "They throw it out." The closing call, "Let anyone who has ears to hear listen," is the one Jesus gave after the parable of the sower (8:8; Mark 4:9).

p: Not ordinary people who were careless about purity, but people known to live outside God's law.
b: Tax collectors gathered tolls and taxes for Herod Antipas or for Rome, and were widely seen as collaborators and cheats (3:12–13; 19:8). Who the "sinners" (ἁμαρτωλοί) were is debated. Joachim Jeremias took the word to include the common people who did not keep the Pharisees' standards of purity. E. P. Sanders argued against him that it means the wicked: people who openly broke God's commandments, lenders at interest, prostitutes and the like, and did not repent; on his view Jesus' meals with them offended because he welcomed them before they had made restitution or offered sacrifice. James Dunn answered that "sinners" was also a factional label, used by stricter groups for other Jews who did not keep the law their way. Luke says these people came "to hear him", the posture of disciples (10:39).

p: The verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling against Moses and God in the desert.
b: Διαγογγύζω, "grumble, mutter," is the word the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, uses for Israel complaining in the wilderness against Moses and Aaron (Exodus 16:2, 7–8; Numbers 14:2). Luke uses it again when the crowd grumbles that Jesus has gone to stay with Zacchaeus, "a sinful man" (19:7). The complaint is that Jesus "takes sinners in" (προσδέχεται, "welcomes, receives as guests") and eats with them: in the Middle East to share a table was to accept a person. The three parables of this chapter are Jesus' answer to this one complaint.

p: Luke says "this parable", singular, though three stories follow.
b: Luke introduces "this parable" in the singular, and then tells three: a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son. Many readers take them as one parable in three panels, each answering the grumbling of 15:2, and each ending with a celebration. The numbers shrink as the stakes rise: one in a hundred, one in ten, one in two. And the last panel has no ending: we do not learn whether the elder son goes in. The singular may also be a Semitic way of speaking (compare 5:36; 6:39).

t: Two tellings of the lost sheep
p: Luke's sheep is "lost", told to critics of Jesus' meals. Matthew's "strays", told to disciples about care in the church.
b: The ἔρημος, "wilderness," was open grazing land, not sand desert; Matthew has "on the hillsides" (Matthew 18:12). A hundred sheep was a fair-sized flock, perhaps owned by a family and herded by more than one shepherd. The two Gospels tell the story to different hearers. In Matthew, Jesus speaks to his disciples about "these little ones" who stray, and ends with God's will that none be lost (Matthew 18:14). In Luke, he answers Pharisees and scribes who object to his meals with sinners, and the sheep is "lost" (ἀπολωλός) and found. Ezekiel 34 pictures God himself as the shepherd who searches for the lost and brings back the strayed (Ezekiel 34:11–16).

a: he lifts it onto his shoulders
t: The shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders
p: One of the earliest Christian pictures of Jesus, painted in the Roman catacombs.
b: A lost sheep often lies down and will not move, so the shepherd carries it, holding its legs at his chest. Isaiah pictures God as a shepherd: "With his arm he will gather up the lambs" (Isaiah 40:11). This image, a young shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders, is one of the oldest Christian pictures of Jesus. It appears in the Roman catacombs of the 200s, long before artists showed the crucifixion, and it borrows the pose of an older Greek statue type, a man carrying a ram. Luke stresses the shepherd's joy: he does the carrying, "full of joy."

a: ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance
p: Is Jesus being ironic about the grumblers, or does he grant that some in Israel are truly righteous?
b: Readers take the phrase in two ways. Many see irony: the Pharisees and scribes think they need no repentance, and Jesus quotes their self-image back at them (compare 16:15; 18:9). Others think Jesus means it plainly: Luke calls Zechariah and Elizabeth "righteous" and blameless (1:6), and Jesus said he came to call sinners, not the righteous (5:32). On this view the parable does not mock the faithful; it asks them to share heaven's joy over the lost instead of resenting it. Amy-Jill Levine reads all three stories as about the joy of finding what was lost, not about repentance at all, since sheep and coins cannot repent; Luke's own lines (15:7, 10) add the lesson about sinners.

p: A drachma was a silver coin worth about a day's wage. Ten was a poor family's savings.
b: The Greek drachma was a silver coin about equal to the Roman denarius, a laborer's pay for a day (Matthew 20:2). Ten drachmas were a modest sum, but for a poor household they might be all the cash it had. A popular explanation says the coins were sewn into the woman's headdress as her dowry, which would make the loss a disgrace; Joachim Jeremias suggested it, but there is little evidence for the custom in Jesus' time, and the story does not need it. Her house, like most village houses, would have had a low door, few or no windows and a floor of beaten earth, which is why she lights a lamp and sweeps.

p: The Greek word for friends is feminine. Jesus pictures God through a woman's search.
b: "Friends" and "neighbors" are feminine in the Greek (τὰς φίλας καὶ γείτονας): she calls the women of the village. Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Simeon and Anna (2:25–38), the widow of Zarephath and Naaman (4:25–27), the mustard seed sown by a man and the yeast hidden by a woman (13:18–21). Here the shepherd and the woman stand side by side, both as pictures of God seeking the lost. Amy-Jill Levine notes that this makes a woman the image of God in a story told to men who would have known Isaiah's picture of God as a mother (Isaiah 66:13).

p: "Before the angels" is a reverent way of saying that God himself rejoices.
b: Jewish speech of the time often avoided naming God directly, saying "heaven" (15:7, 18) or "before the angels" instead (compare 12:8–9). The joy here is God's own, shared by the heavenly court. Luke's whole Gospel is full of joy at God's saving acts: at the births (1:14, 44, 58; 2:10), at the disciples' return (10:17, 20), and at the end, in the temple (24:52). The parables of this chapter end, each one, with a call to rejoice together.
orig: ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ (enōpion tōn angelōn tou theou), 'in the presence of God's angels'

t: Two sons, and the younger one
p: Hearers who knew Genesis expected the younger son to be the favored one: Abel, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim.
b: The opening line would make Jewish hearers think of the stories of brothers in Genesis: Cain and Abel, Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, Joseph and his brothers, Manasseh and Ephraim. Again and again God favors the younger, and the elder resents it. In Jesus' story the younger son earns no favor at all, and the elder son has done nothing wrong except refuse to rejoice. English calls it "the parable of the prodigal son", but the Gospel gives it no title, and many readers now call it the parable of the father, or of the two sons, since the father is the one figure in every scene.
r: Genesis 4:1–8; Genesis 25:23; Genesis 27; Genesis 37; Genesis 48:13–20; Matthew 21:28–32

a: give me the part of the estate that falls to me
p: By law the younger of two sons received a third. Asking for it early shamed the family, most readers think.
b: Under Deuteronomy 21:17 the firstborn received "a double share," so the younger of two sons would get a third. A father could divide property before his death, but the wise man Ben Sira advised a father not to hand over his property while he lived (Sirach 33:20–24). Kenneth Bailey argued from Middle Eastern village life that such a request meant "I wish you were dead." Amy-Jill Levine replies that the text says nothing of shame and that gifts during a father's life are well attested. Either way, the father gives the younger son what he asks, and divides "his living" (τὸν βίον, literally "his life") between both sons: the elder also receives his share (15:31).

p: The Greek says he lived wastefully. The prostitutes are the elder brother's charge (15:30), not the narrator's.
b: The adverb ἀσώτως comes from a word for a person who cannot save, a spendthrift. It does not by itself mean sexual sin. English "prodigal" comes from the Latin prodigus, "wasteful," used in later titles for the parable. The narrator says only that he "scattered" his estate; it is the elder brother who later claims he spent it "with prostitutes" (15:30), and the reader cannot tell whether he knows or assumes. The "faraway country" means Gentile land, far from his people, which prepares for the pigs.

t: The lowest a Jewish son could fall
p: Pigs were unclean animals. For a Jewish hearer, a son feeding a Gentile's pigs had hit bottom.
b: The Law calls the pig unclean (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8), and the Mishnah says that pigs may not be raised anywhere in the land of Israel (Mishnah Bava Kamma 7:7). Pigs belonged to Gentiles, as in the story of the man possessed by demons near Gerasa (8:32–33). The son has "latched on" (ἐκολλήθη, "glued himself") to a Gentile who has no use for him but this. For Jesus' hearers the picture said everything: he has lost his money, his family, his people and his purity.

a: the carob pods the pigs were eating
p: The pods of the carob tree were fodder for animals and food for the very poor.
b: Κεράτια, "little horns," are the curved pods of the carob tree, sweet and fibrous, fed to animals and eaten by the poorest people in hard times. Joachim Jeremias cites a later rabbinic saying that "when Israel is reduced to carob pods, they repent" (Leviticus Rabbah 35:6). Later Christian legend held that John the Baptist's "locusts" were carob pods, so the carob is still called "Saint John's bread." No one gives the son anything, not even the pigs' food: in the text followed here (see the variant), the same verb, "eat his fill," describes Lazarus at the rich man's gate (16:21).

t: Repentance, or a plan to eat?
p: Does the son truly repent, or does he work out a scheme to get fed? Readers differ.
b: "He came to himself" can describe a change of heart; a similar phrase is used for repentance in Jewish writings, and Christian preaching has long treated this verse as the moment of conversion. But his first thought is food, and his plan is to come back as a hired worker, an outsider paid by the day, who could earn back what he lost. Kenneth Bailey argued that he is still trying to save himself, and that the real turning comes when he accepts his father's welcome. Others think it reads too much into a short story to deny the son's sincerity. Either way, the father does not wait to examine his motives.

t: A confession, and an echo of Pharaoh?
p: "Against heaven" means against God. The words also echo Pharaoh's confession to Moses.
b: "Heaven" is a reverent way of saying God (15:7). The son confesses a sin against God and against his father, as the Law joined the two in the command to honor parents. Kenneth Bailey heard in the words an echo of Pharaoh, who said in a tight spot, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you" (Exodus 10:16), and took it as a sign that the son was rehearsing a useful speech. Most readers simply hear a true confession, like David's "You, you alone, are the one I sinned against" (Psalm 51:4). The father cuts off the speech before the request to be made a hired man (15:21).

a: his heart went out to him
p: The verb is the one used for Jesus at Nain and for the Samaritan on the road: compassion felt in the body.
b: Σπλαγχνίζομαι comes from σπλάγχνα, the inner organs, which ancient people saw as the seat of feeling. Luke uses it three times: of Jesus seeing the widow of Nain (7:13), of the Samaritan seeing the wounded man (10:33), and of this father. Each time, someone sees, is moved, and acts. The father has been watching for his son, and sees him "still far away."

a: He ran, fell on his son's neck and kissed him again and again
p: The words closely echo the Greek of Genesis 33:4, where Esau runs to meet the brother who wronged him.
b: The father's welcome closely echoes the Septuagint at Genesis 33:4, where Esau, whom Jacob had cheated, "ran to meet him, hugged him, fell on his neck and kissed him" (Genesis 33:4); compare Joseph with his brothers and his father (Genesis 45:14; 46:29). Luke's verb, καταφιλέω, is a strengthened "kiss": "again and again" is one way to take it, "warmly" another. In those stories the wronged party forgives. Kenneth Bailey adds that a dignified older man in a village did not run, since running meant hitching up his robe and showing his legs (compare Sirach 19:30, on how a man's walk shows who he is). The father takes the shame on himself, in front of the village, before anyone can shame his son.

p: Each gift restores him: the robe honors him, the ring gives him authority, sandals mark a son, not a slave.
b: The father says nothing to his son. He speaks to the slaves, and each order answers the son's planned request to be made a hired man. The best robe (literally "the first robe") is a guest of honor's garment, perhaps the father's own. A ring could be a signet ring, a sign of authority to act for the family, as when "Pharaoh slipped the signet ring off his own hand and set it on Joseph's hand" (Genesis 41:42). Sandals marked a free man; slaves went barefoot. Church fathers read each gift as a figure. Jerome (Letter 21) took the ring as a seal and the fattened calf as Christ himself; the robe was read in various fathers as the garment of the Spirit, or of baptism.

a: Fetch the calf we've been fattening and slaughter it
t: A feast for the whole village
p: A grain-fed calf was meat for a hundred people or more. This is a public celebration.
b: Most families ate meat rarely, and a calf kept in a stall and fed grain was saved for a great occasion. One calf would feed a large gathering, so the party was for the whole village, a public sign that the son was received back. The verb "slaughter" (θύω) is also the word for offering a sacrifice, though here it means a festive meal. The merrymaking (εὐφραίνω) answers the grumbling of 15:2: this is the meal with a sinner that Jesus' critics objected to.

a: was dead, and he has come back to life
p: In the father's eyes, the son who left was as good as dead. The words later describe conversion.
b: The son had not died, but to his father he had been as one dead, lost to the family. The verb ἀναζάω, "live again," is used of returning life; the New Testament letters use the same picture for conversion: "you were dead in your trespasses" and God "made you alive" (Ephesians 2:1, 5; Romans 6:13). The refrain, "was dead ... has come back to life ... was lost ... has been found," ties this story to the lost sheep and coin, and is repeated to the elder brother at the end (15:32).

p: In Luke's setting, he stands for the grumblers of 15:2. Later readers made him "the Jews", a reading Jewish scholars reject.
b: The frame of the chapter points to the Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus ate with sinners (15:2): like the elder son, they have served faithfully and resent the welcome of the unworthy. Some church fathers took the two sons as Israel and the Gentiles, the elder being the Jewish people who would not join the feast. Jerome's letter on this parable discusses both readings (Letter 21). Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine point out that this turns a story about one family into a judgment on a whole people, and that the father's last words to the elder son are tender: "My child, you are with me all the time, and all I have belongs to you" (15:31). The father goes out to him as he went out to the younger.

a: I have worked like a slave for you
t: A son who sees himself as a slave
p: The elder son speaks of his years at home as slave labor, and never calls his father "Father".
b: The verb δουλεύω means to serve as a slave. The younger son planned to come back as a hired man; the elder son, who never left, describes his life at home as slavery. He does not address his father as "Father," as the younger son did (15:12, 18, 21), and he calls his brother "this son of yours" (15:30). A young goat was a much smaller gift than a fattened calf. The father's answer, "My child" (τέκνον), corrects him gently: he has been a son all along, and everything is his.

t: "This son of yours", "this brother of yours"
p: The elder son will not call him "my brother". The father answers, "this brother of yours".
b: The elder son disowns his brother: "this son of yours." The father's reply turns the words around: "this brother of yours" (15:32). The charge about prostitutes is the elder son's alone; the narrator had said only that the younger son scattered his estate (15:13). "Gobbled up your living" uses βίος again, the father's livelihood (15:12): the elder son speaks as if the property were still his father's, though he himself already holds the rest of it (15:31).

a: It was right to be merry and glad
p: We never learn whether the elder son goes in. The hearers of 15:2 must finish the story themselves.
b: "It was right" translates ἔδει, "it was necessary," Luke's word for what God's plan requires (2:49; 13:16; 19:5; 24:26). The father's joy is not optional. The parable stops with the elder son outside the door, and Jesus does not say whether he goes in. The Pharisees and scribes of 15:2 are left to decide whether they will join the meal with sinners. The book of Jonah ends the same way, with an angry, righteous man outside a celebration of mercy and God's question unanswered (Jonah 4:10–11); Timothy Keller develops the comparison at length. Note the small change from 15:24: the younger son "came back to life" there; here, speaking to the brother, the father says he "has come to life" (ἔζησεν). Christian art has given the parable its best-known image in Rembrandt's late painting The Return of the Prodigal Son (about 1668), with the elder son standing apart.
l: The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt)
The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt)

a: A rich man had a manager
p: An οἰκονόμος ran a rich man's property, often as a slave or freedman, with power to make deals in his name.
b: Large estates were run by managers who rented out land, collected the owner's share of the harvest, lent and kept the accounts. Such a manager might be a trusted slave or a freedman, and he acted as the owner's legal agent, so the contracts he signed were binding. Luke uses the same word for the manager in charge of the household in 12:42. The charge was "reported" with the verb διαβάλλω, from which comes διάβολος, "slanderer, devil": it may have been malicious, but the manager does not deny it.

a: Hand over the books of your management
p: The manager has lost his job but still holds the accounts, and his signature still binds his master.
b: "Hand over the books" is literally "give back the account (λόγος) of your management." The master's decision is made; the manager has only the time it takes to close the books. Kenneth Bailey notes that the master does not jail him or demand repayment, which is itself an act of mercy, and that the manager does not try to defend himself. In that short window his acts are still legally the master's acts, and that is what his scheme relies on.

a: Digging is too hard for me, and begging would shame me
t: Too weak to dig, too proud to beg
p: An office worker could not survive as a day laborer, and begging was the last disgrace.
b: Digging was the hardest kind of day labor, and a man used to keeping accounts was not fit for it. Begging was worse: "better to die than to beg," said Ben Sira (Sirach 40:28). The manager's honest self-assessment drives his plan. He needs friends who will owe him a place in their homes (16:4), which is the hinge of Jesus' lesson in 16:9: "they will take you into the everlasting tents."

a: A hundred baths of olive oil
p: A bath was roughly 6 to 10 gallons; a cor was ten baths. These are big debts, owed by tenants or merchants.
b: The bath was a Hebrew liquid measure; estimates of its size run from about 22 to about 39 liters (6 to 10 gallons), and Josephus implies the higher figure (Antiquities 8.57), and the cor (Hebrew kor) was ten baths, a dry measure for grain (Ezekiel 45:11, 14). A hundred baths of oil is the yield of a large olive grove; a hundred cors of wheat, the harvest of a large farm. The debtors may be tenant farmers who owed the owner a share of their crop, or merchants buying on credit. Joachim Jeremias reckoned that the two reductions were worth about the same, some five hundred denarii each, a laborer's wages for well over a year.

p: Plain English Translation fraud, his own commission, or interest the Law forbade? Each reading changes the story.
b: Readers have offered four explanations. (1) The manager simply cheats his master once more, and Jesus praises only his quick wits. (2) He cuts his own commission, the amount he had added for himself, so he loses money but wins friends (Joseph Fitzmyer). (3) He removes interest hidden in the bills, since the Law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite (Deuteronomy 23:19); J. D. M. Derrett noted that the larger cut on oil (half) than on wheat (a fifth) fits the higher rates charged on oil. (4) Kenneth Bailey argued that the villagers think the generous master ordered the reductions, so the master cannot reverse them without losing honor, and the manager gambles on his master's goodness. See the chapter page.

a: the master praised the crooked manager
p: "The master" may be the rich man in the story, or Jesus, whom Luke calls "the Lord". Where does the parable end?
b: The Greek ὁ κύριος can mean "the master" or "the Lord." Most interpreters think it is the rich man, who grudgingly admires the scheme that has outwitted him. Joachim Jeremias argued that it is Jesus, since Luke elsewhere uses "the Lord" for Jesus at the close of a parable (18:6: "the Lord said"). Either way, the praise is for shrewdness, not dishonesty. "The crooked manager" is literally "the manager of injustice," a Hebrew-style phrase like "the judge of injustice" in 18:6. Scholars also disagree where the parable ends and Jesus' comments begin: after 16:7, 16:8a, 16:8b or 16:9. 16:9–13 look like a string of sayings about money gathered around the story.
orig: ὁ κύριος (ho kyrios), 'the master' or 'the Lord'

p: The same word describes the faithful manager of 12:42. This one has the cleverness without the faithfulness.
b: Φρονίμως, "shrewdly," and φρόνιμος, "shrewd," are the words used for the manager "who is faithful and sensible" in 12:42, the same word for "manager" (οἰκονόμος) and the same quality. Elsewhere this translation renders φρόνιμος "sensible" where it means good sense (Matthew 7:24; 24:45; 25:2) and "shrewd" where it means worldly cleverness, as here. The manager of 12:42 has both qualities; this one has only the second, and 16:10–12 at once demands the first: "Someone who is faithful in the smallest things is faithful in big things as well." "Toward their own kind" is literally "into their own generation": people of this age deal cleverly with one another.

p: The Qumran scrolls divide the world into "sons of light" and "sons of darkness". So do Paul and John.
b: "Children (sons) of this age" and "children of light" are Hebrew-style phrases for people who belong to something. The Dead Sea Scrolls call the faithful community "the sons of light" and their enemies "the sons of darkness" (Community Rule 1:9–10; War Scroll 1:1). The New Testament uses the same language for believers (John 12:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:5; Ephesians 5:8). Jesus' complaint is that people of this world plan more cleverly for their futures than God's people plan for theirs.
r: John 12:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:5; Ephesians 5:8; Community Rule 1:9–10; War Scroll 1:1; 20:34–36

p: Μαμωνᾶς is Aramaic for "wealth, property". The KJV kept it as "mammon". It is not the name of a demon.
b: Μαμωνᾶς is the Aramaic word mamona, "wealth, possessions," which the KJV kept as "mammon" (16:9, 11, 13; Matthew 6:24). It is not a god or a demon in the Gospels, though medieval writers turned it into one, and Milton's Paradise Lost made Mammon a fallen angel. "The wealth of dishonesty" may mean money gained unjustly, or money as such, which belongs to this unjust age and is never fully clean. The Parables of Enoch have the rich say, "Our souls are full of the wealth of wrongdoing" (1 Enoch 63:10), and George Nickelsburg has shown how closely Luke's warnings to the rich resemble those in 1 Enoch 92–105.
orig: μαμωνᾶς τῆς ἀδικίας (mamōnas tēs adikias), 'the wealth of injustice'

p: The manager wanted homes to go to. Jesus speaks of the tents of the age to come.
b: The manager wanted debtors to "take me into their own homes" (16:4); Jesus' application uses the same verb for being received into "the everlasting tents." Tents recall Israel's journey in the wilderness and the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in shelters and remembered God's care (Leviticus 23:42–43), a feast later linked with the age to come (Zechariah 14:16). "They" who receive may be the friends made with money, the poor who were helped, or a reverent way of saying God, as in 12:20 ("they demand your life"). John Wesley's sermon on this text, "The Use of Money" (1760), summed it up: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.

p: The same principle governs the parable of the minas: faithfulness in a little leads to charge of much.
b: Jesus turns from shrewdness to faithfulness. Money is "the smallest thing"; "the real thing" (16:11) and "what is yours" (16:12) are the riches of the kingdom, which God gives to those who were trustworthy with what was only lent to them. The parable of the minas makes the same point: "You were faithful over a very little, so you will have authority over ten towns" (19:17; compare Matthew 25:21). Everything a person owns in this life is "what belongs to another," held in trust from God.

a: No household slave can be a slave to two masters
p: The saying is in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount. Luke adds "household slave", tying it to the manager.
b: Matthew 6:24 has the same saying word for word in Greek, except that Luke begins "no household slave" (οἰκέτης). That small word links the saying to the manager of the parable, himself a servant of a master. A slave owned by two masters could not serve both fully; when they disagreed, he would have to choose. Jesus treats wealth as a rival master that demands service, the way the prophets spoke of idols. See the note on Matthew 6:24.

a: since they were fond of money
t: Were the Pharisees lovers of money?
p: Luke's charge is a stock accusation of the time. Josephus says the Pharisees lived simply.
b: "Lovers of money" (φιλάργυροι) was a standard charge in ancient debates: Greek philosophers used it against rival teachers, and 2 Timothy 3:2 lists it among the vices of the last days. Josephus, who says he followed the Pharisees' rule in public life (Life 12), says the Pharisees "live simply, despising delicacies" (Antiquities 18.12). Many Pharisees were tradesmen and farmers, not wealthy. Luke's picture reflects his own sharp contrast between money and God, and his polemic with the Pharisees of his day; it should not be taken as a fair description of the whole movement. Luke also shows Pharisees who are open to Jesus (7:36; 13:31; Acts 5:34; 15:5).

p: Βδέλυγμα is the Greek Bible's word for Hebrew to'evah, the "abhorrent" thing God hates.
b: Βδέλυγμα translates Hebrew to'evah in the Septuagint, the word for what God finds abhorrent, from idols (Deuteronomy 7:25) to a proud heart: "The LORD finds every haughty heart abhorrent" (Proverbs 16:5). The same word stands in "the abomination of desolation" (Mark 13:14). "God knows your hearts" recalls what the LORD told Samuel: "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). To "justify yourselves" is to declare yourselves in the right, as the lawyer did in 10:29 and the Pharisee in the temple in 18:11–12.

a: The Law and the Prophets lasted until John
p: Hans Conzelmann built a theory of Luke's whole plan of history on this verse.
b: The verse has no verb in the first half: "The Law and the Prophets until John." Matthew has the saying in another form (Matthew 11:12–13). Hans Conzelmann argued that it shows Luke's plan of history in three periods: Israel up to John, the time of Jesus, and the time of the church. Many later scholars think the scheme too neat, and note that Luke counts John both as the last of the prophets (7:26–28) and as the first to announce the good news (3:18). The next verse insists that the Law is not abolished (16:17): what has changed is that the kingdom is now being announced.

a: everyone is pressing their way into it
t: Pressing in, or pressed to come in?
p: The verb can mean "forces his way in", "is pressed to enter" or "uses violence against it".
b: Βιάζεται can be read three ways. (1) Middle voice: everyone is forcing or pressing their way in, with eager zeal, as the tax collectors and sinners do (15:1). Most translations take it this way. (2) Passive: everyone is urged, pressed to come in, as the master's slave was told to "make them come in" (14:23). (3) Hostile: everyone treats it with violence, which would match Matthew's form, where the kingdom "is under violent attack" (Matthew 11:12). "Everyone" is an overstatement in any case, since many refuse (7:30).

a: one tiny hook of a letter could fall from the Law
t: Not a stroke of the Law
p: Luke keeps the saying Matthew puts in the Sermon on the Mount: the Law still stands.
b: The κεραία, "little horn," was a tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another, as the hook on ד (d) from ר (r). Matthew has the saying in his Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:18). In Luke it guards against misreading 16:16: the time of the Law and the Prophets has given way to the announcement of the kingdom, but the Law is not cancelled. Jacob Jervell argued that Luke, of all the Gospel writers, is most concerned to show that Jesus and the first believers kept the Law (2:22–24, 39; 23:56; Acts 21:20–24).

a: Everyone who divorces his wife and marries someone else commits adultery
t: Divorce, and why it stands here
p: Luke's form has no exception clause. It shows that the Law's demand stands, made stricter, not looser.
b: In Jewish law a man could divorce his wife by giving her a written document (Deuteronomy 24:1–4); the schools of Hillel and Shammai debated the grounds (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Jesus' saying, here and in Mark 10:11–12, forbids remarriage after divorce, with no exception; Matthew adds "except for sexual sin" (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Luke speaks only of the man: he who divorces and remarries, and he who marries a divorced woman. Placed after 16:17, the saying shows a case where Jesus' teaching is stricter than Moses, not looser. Some see a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who divorced to marry Herodias (3:19). For the churches' different teaching on divorce and remarriage, see the cards at Matthew 5:32 and 19:3–12.

a: He dressed in purple and fine linen
p: Purple was the costliest dye in the world, and fine linen the best cloth. He dressed like a king.
b: Purple dye came from murex shellfish gathered near Tyre, and it took thousands of shells to dye one garment; purple was the color of kings and the very rich. Βύσσος was fine Egyptian linen, often worn as an undergarment. The woman of strength in Proverbs wears both ("Fine linen and purple are what she wears," Proverbs 31:22), but she made them with her own hands, and of her it is also said, "She spreads her palm open to the poor" (Proverbs 31:20). "He made merry" (εὐφραινόμενος) is the verb of the father's feast in 15:23–32: one feast welcomes the lost, the other shuts the gate. Revelation dresses Babylon in the same goods (Revelation 18:12, 16).

t: The only invented parable character with a name
p: Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar, "God has helped". The rich man has no name.
b: Lazarus is the only invented character in Jesus' parables to be given a name (Abraham, the other named figure, is the patriarch). Lazarus (Λάζαρος) is a short Greek form of the Hebrew Eleazar, "God has helped": no one else helps him. The rich man is never named; Latin readers later called him Dives, simply the Latin for "rich man," and one early papyrus gives him a name (see the variant on 16:19). Some scholars connect this Lazarus with Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus raised from the dead (John 11), because of the closing words about someone rising from the dead (16:31). Medieval Europe made the poor Lazarus the patron of the sick, which is why a leper was once called a "lazar" and a quarantine hospital a "lazaretto."
orig: Λάζαρος (Lazaros), from Hebrew Eleazar, 'God has helped'

p: Street dogs were scavengers and unclean. Their licking is either one more humiliation or the only comfort he gets.
b: The dogs are not pets but the half-wild scavengers of every ancient town, unclean animals that ate whatever was thrown out (1 Kings 21:19; Psalm 22:16). Most readers take their licking as one more humiliation: Lazarus is too weak to drive them off. Some see a bitter irony: the dogs show him more attention than the rich man does. Lazarus "longed to eat his fill" with the same verb as the younger son longing for the pigs' pods (15:16). The Byzantine text adds that he wanted "the scraps" (see the variant).

a: carried off by the angels to Abraham's embrace
p: The picture is a banquet: Lazarus reclines in the place of honor beside Abraham, the host.
b: Κόλπος means chest or lap. At a banquet, guests reclined on their left elbows, and the one nearest the host lay with his head close to the host's chest, as the beloved disciple lay "in Jesus' embrace" (John 13:23; compare John 1:18). Lazarus, who ate nothing at the rich man's table, now has the place of honor at Abraham's feast (13:28–29; Matthew 8:11). Jewish writings spoke of the righteous dead being received by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (4 Maccabees 13:17). The Latin funeral rite still sings, as the body leaves the church, "May the angels lead you into paradise ... and with Lazarus, who once was poor, may you have eternal rest." The rich man "was buried," no doubt with honor; nothing is said of Lazarus' burial.

t: Hades: the place of the dead
p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol. Here it holds the wicked dead in torment, apart from the righteous.
b: In the Septuagint ᾅδης translates Sheol, the Hebrew world of the dead. In older parts of the Old Testament all the dead go to Sheol, good and bad alike. By Jesus' time many Jews pictured the dead kept in separate places until the judgment. 1 Enoch 22, written centuries before, describes hollow places for the spirits of the dead, with "the spring of water with light above it" for the righteous (1 Enoch 22:9), while "a place has been made for sinners when they die and are buried in the earth" (1 Enoch 22:10). Luke's Hades is a place of torment, with Abraham's company within sight. It is not Gehenna, the final judgment after the resurrection (12:5). How far this parable describes the actual state of the dead is debated; see the card on this chapter's page.

p: The rich man claims Abraham as father. John the Baptist had warned against trusting that.
b: The rich man calls Abraham "Father," and Abraham calls him "My child" (16:25): the family tie is real, but it does not save him. John the Baptist had warned the crowds not to rely on having Abraham as their father (3:8; compare John 8:39). Luke later calls the bent woman and Zacchaeus children of Abraham (13:16; 19:9), people others despised. The rich man still treats Lazarus as a servant to be sent on errands (16:24, 27). A drop of water on the tongue is all he asks; compare the thirst of the rich in a story told in the Jerusalem Talmud (see the chapter page).

a: you got your good things in full during your life
p: The rich man has already received his good things, as Jesus warned the rich in 6:24.
b: The verb ἀπέλαβες means "you received (in full, or as your due)." It echoes the woe on the rich in 6:24, who "have received" their comfort already, though there the verb is a different one, ἀπέχετε, used on receipts for "paid in full." The parable acts out Mary's song (1:53: the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty) and the blessings and woes of 6:20–26. Abraham does not say the rich man was cruel or that Lazarus was pious. The story's charge comes later: the rich man and his brothers did not listen to Moses and the Prophets (16:29–31), who command, "Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11). His sin was the man at his gate he never saw.

a: a huge gulf has been set firm
p: After death, Abraham says, no one can cross. The verse has played a large part in debates over purgatory.
b: The χάσμα is fixed by God ("has been set firm" is a divine passive). 1 Enoch also pictures the dead kept apart in separate places (1 Enoch 22:9–13). Christians have drawn different conclusions. Protestant confessions cite this parable (Westminster Confession 32.1 lists 16:23–24) to show that a person's state is fixed at death, so there is no purgatory and no change after death; Catholic teachers reply that the parable concerns the righteous and the wicked, not those being purified, and Catholic tradition placed the souls of the righteous before Christ in "Abraham's bosom" (Catechism 633). Orthodox teaching prays for the dead while keeping that the final state is fixed at the judgment. See the card on this chapter's page.

t: A priestly family in purple and linen?
p: An old minority reading heard in the rich man and his five brothers the house of Annas, whose five sons became high priests.
b: This is an old suggestion, not something the text says. Already in the 19th century Friedrich Lisco reported that some expositors "referred it to the family of Annas and his son-in-law, Caiaphas," and the reading is still repeated in popular commentary. Josephus says that the high priest Annas had five sons, all of whom held the high priesthood after him (Antiquities 20.198), and his son-in-law Caiaphas was high priest in Jesus' day (3:2). Priests wore linen and the high priest's robes had purple in them (Exodus 28:5–6). The high-priestly party were Sadducees, who held to Moses and denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), and in Acts they are "deeply upset" at preaching about resurrection from the dead (Acts 4:2). A rich man in purple and linen with five brothers, who are told "Moses and the Prophets" and will not be persuaded "if someone rises from the dead," fits that family strikingly. Most interpreters do not adopt the reading: the parable is about any rich man who ignores the poor at his gate, and nothing in it requires a particular family.

p: The verb is the one Acts uses for the apostles' solemn testimony.
b: Διαμαρτύρομαι, "testify solemnly, warn," is one of Luke's words for preaching in Acts: Peter "testified" at Pentecost (Acts 2:40) and Paul "testified" to Jews and Greeks (Acts 20:21, 24). The rich man wants a messenger from the dead to do what the apostles will later do. Abraham's answer, and the book of Acts, show that even the testimony of one raised from the dead does not compel belief.

a: They have Moses and the Prophets
t: Moses and the Prophets are enough
p: The Law and the Prophets already demand care for the poor. Luke ends his Gospel by returning to them.
b: "Moses and the Prophets" means the Jewish Scriptures. They speak plainly about the poor: open your hand to the needy (Deuteronomy 15:7–11), share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house (Isaiah 58:7), and woe to those who lie on ivory beds and feast on lambs while ignoring the ruin of their people (Amos 6:4–7). The rich man's brothers do not need a ghost; they need to read. At the end of the Gospel the risen Jesus himself opens "Moses and all the prophets" to the disciples (24:27, 44), and Luke's readers knew that the resurrection did not convince everyone.

a: not even if someone rises from the dead will they be persuaded
p: Christian readers think of Jesus' own resurrection, and of Lazarus of Bethany, after whom the plotting began.
b: In the story the rich man asks only for a messenger from the dead. But Luke's readers knew of one who "rose from the dead," Jesus himself (24:6, 46), and that many still did not believe (Acts 17:32; 26:8). John's Gospel tells of a man named Lazarus who was raised, after which the leaders did not repent but plotted: "So the chief priests decided to kill Lazarus too" (John 12:10). Some scholars think the two stories grew from one tradition; others think the shared name is a coincidence. Either way, Luke's point is that the problem is not lack of evidence but a closed heart.

a: There is no way that snares will not come
p: A σκάνδαλον is the trigger of a trap: whatever makes a person fall away from faith.
b: Σκάνδαλον was the trigger stick of a trap, then anything that makes a person stumble or fall, and in the Gospels whatever causes someone to give up faith or to sin. This site renders it "snare" and the verb σκανδαλίζω "trip up," as in Matthew 18:6–7. Jesus says snares are bound to come in a fallen world, yet the person who sets them is still responsible. Luke has the saying without Matthew's setting of a child placed among the disciples (Matthew 18:1–7).

t: A millstone, and the little ones
p: Drowning with a stone tied on was a known punishment. The "little ones" are weak or humble believers.
b: Luke's Greek has "a mill stone" (λίθος μυλικός), where Matthew and Mark have "a donkey's millstone," the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by an animal (Matthew 18:6; Mark 9:42); later copyists of Luke made it match (see the variant). Drowning with a weight was a punishment known in the Roman world. In Luke no child is in view: "these little ones" are disciples who are weak or humble, the kind of people the Pharisees despised (15:2) and the kind who could be led away by others' bad example. Better to die than to cause one of them to fall.

p: The Law commanded rebuking a neighbor instead of hating him in secret. Jesus joins it to forgiveness.
b: Leviticus joins the two commands: "Do not hate your brother in your heart. Be sure to correct your fellow citizen" (Leviticus 19:17). The Qumran community made it a rule to rebuke a member truthfully, humbly and kindly, on the same day, and not to bring a charge before the assembly without first rebuking him before witnesses (Community Rule 5:24–6:1). Jesus' version is short: rebuke, and if he repents, forgive. Matthew turns it into a process for the church (Matthew 18:15–17). "Keep watch over yourselves" may close 17:1–2 or open this saying.

p: Luke's "seven times in one day" and Matthew's "seventy-seven times" both mean: without limit.
b: In Matthew, Peter offers seven times and Jesus answers "seventy-seven times," reversing Lamech's boast: "Cain will be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy and seven" (Genesis 4:24; Matthew 18:21–22). Luke's form, seven times in a single day, makes the same point in a different way: if the same person wrongs you and asks forgiveness seven times before sunset, you still forgive. Here forgiveness answers the words "I repent." Whether Christians must forgive someone who does not repent is debated; Jesus prays for his executioners on the cross in many manuscripts of 23:34, and Stephen does the same (Acts 7:60).

a: The apostles said to the Lord
p: Luke, unlike Mark, often calls Jesus "the Lord" in his own narration.
b: Mark almost never calls Jesus "the Lord" in the narration; Luke often does (7:13, 19; 10:1, 39, 41; 13:15; 18:6; 19:8; 22:61; 24:3), and the disciples confess "The Lord really has been raised!" (24:34). The narrator writes from the faith of the church, which confessed the risen Jesus as Lord (Acts 2:36). "The apostles" are the Twelve, whom Jesus named apostles (6:13). Their request, literally "Add faith to us," follows the hard demand to forgive without limit: they feel they do not have the faith for it.

t: A mustard seed and a mulberry tree
p: The black mulberry has deep, strong roots. A tree planted in the sea is a deliberately impossible picture.
b: Συκάμινος is usually the black mulberry, a tree with deep, tough roots, though the Septuagint uses the same word for the sycomore fig (1 Kings 10:27; Amos 7:14). Luke uses a different word for Zacchaeus' sycomore (19:4). In Matthew a mountain moves (Matthew 17:20; 21:21; compare Mark 11:23). A tree planted in the sea is meant to be absurd: faith even "the size of a mustard seed," the smallest seed a Galilean knew (13:19), is enough for what seems impossible, because it is God who acts. The apostles asked for more faith; Jesus answers that the question is not how much, but whether they trust God at all.

a: with a slave out plowing or minding the flock
t: A small farmer and his one slave
p: Jesus pictures a farmer with a single slave who works the field and the kitchen. The hearers took slavery as normal.
b: The picture is of a modest farmer who owns one slave, who plows and herds by day and cooks and serves in the evening. Jesus' hearers took this as an ordinary part of life, and the parable draws on it without approving or condemning it. Modern readers rightly feel the hardness of the picture; see the topic on slavery. The parable's point is not how masters should treat slaves, but how disciples should think about their service to God: they have no claim on him. In 12:37 Jesus gives the opposite picture, a master who comes home and serves his slaves.

a: Tie up your robe and serve me
p: Slaves tucked up their long robes to work. In 12:37 the returning master does this himself to serve his slaves.
b: Περιζώννυμι means to tie up a long robe with a belt so as to move freely for work or travel (Exodus 12:11). This master expects his slave to do it. Luke's readers had already heard of another master who comes home, ties up his robe, seats his slaves at the table and serves them himself (12:37). At the Last Supper Jesus says that he is among the disciples as one who serves (22:27), and in John he ties a towel around himself and washes the disciples' feet (John 13:4–5). The parable describes what disciples owe; the Gospel shows what their Lord gives.

p: The KJV says "unprofitable servants". The point is not that they are worthless, but that they have earned no credit.
b: Ἀχρεῖος means "useless, unprofitable"; Matthew uses it for the slave who buried his master's money (Matthew 25:30). Here, though, the slaves have done everything they were told. The word cannot mean that they did nothing useful; it means they have no claim, no credit beyond what they owed. Some scholars think it means only "mere slaves." The verse became important in the debate over merit. The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles cite it against "works of supererogation," good deeds beyond what God requires (Article 14); Catholic teaching on merit answers that God crowns his own gifts. See the card on this chapter's page.

a: the country between Samaria and Galilee
p: The phrase is unusual, and Luke's geography here has been debated. A border road east toward the Jordan fits.
b: The critical editions read διὰ μέσον, most naturally "between"; the Byzantine text has διὰ μέσου, "through the middle of" (KJV "through the midst of Samaria and Galilee"; see the variant). Since he is heading south to Jerusalem, naming Samaria first is odd. Hans Conzelmann took it as a sign that Luke had only a vague idea of the land's map. Others take it as "between Samaria and Galilee," along the border, through the Jezreel Valley toward Scythopolis (Beth Shean) and down the Jordan valley, the route many Galilean pilgrims took to avoid Samaria, which brings Jesus to Jericho (18:35). A mixed border area also explains a group of men with skin disease that included a Samaritan.

p: The Law required people with skin disease to live apart and warn others away.
b: Leviticus required a person with skin disease to live apart: "He is to live alone, and his home is to be outside the camp" (Leviticus 13:46; compare Numbers 5:2–3). In towns this meant living outside the walls and calling out a warning. Their shared exclusion brings together a Samaritan and Jews who would not otherwise mix. The Greek λεπρός is rendered "a man with skin disease": it covered several skin conditions, not only what is now called Hansen's disease (see the note on 5:12 and the topic).

p: Ἐπιστάτης, "master, chief", is a word only Luke uses, and elsewhere only disciples say it.
b: Luke alone uses ἐπιστάτα, "Master," a Greek title for a person in charge. Everywhere else in Luke it is on the lips of disciples, usually Peter (5:5; 8:24, 45; 9:33, 49). The ten men use a disciple's word, and the plea "show us mercy" (ἐλέησον) is the one the blind man will shout near Jericho (18:38–39). They ask for mercy, not specifically for healing; Jesus' answer gives both.

a: Go and let the priests see you
p: A priest had to inspect a person healed of skin disease and declare him clean (Leviticus 14). They go before they are healed.
b: The Law of cleansing for skin disease required a priest to examine the healed person and declare him clean, followed by offerings over eight days (Leviticus 14:1–32). Jesus gave the same order to the man he healed in 5:14 (compare Mark 1:44; Matthew 8:4). Here, though, the men are sent before anything has happened, and they are made clean "while they were going," as Naaman was told to go and wash before he saw any change (2 Kings 5:10–14). For a Samaritan, "the priests" would mean the Samaritan priesthood at Mount Gerizim, not the temple in Jerusalem. Dennis Hamm argues that this is the point of the story: the Samaritan alone sees that the place where God is to be thanked is no longer Gerizim or Jerusalem but Jesus himself, as Jesus tells the Samaritan woman in John 4:21–24, and so he turns back to give glory to God at Jesus' feet. Jesus sends the men to the Law's own procedure: the healing is meant to bring them back into their communities.

a: giving glory to God at the top of his voice
p: In Luke, people who see God at work answer by glorifying God. Here only one does.
b: "Giving glory to God" (δοξάζων τὸν θεόν) is Luke's regular response to God's saving acts: the shepherds (2:20), the paralyzed man and the crowd (5:25–26), the crowd at Nain (7:16), the bent woman (13:13), the blind man near Jericho (18:43), and the centurion at the cross (23:47). Ten were cleansed; one saw what had happened, turned back and gave God glory. Seeing is the hinge: the verb "saw" (ἰδών) is used of Jesus seeing them (17:14) and of this man seeing that he was healed.

p: The grateful man is a Samaritan, like the good neighbor of 10:33. Luke's hearers knew the bitter feud.
b: Jews and Samaritans had been enemies for centuries, divided over the temple on Mount Gerizim (destroyed by John Hyrcanus in the late 100s BC), over Scripture and over who were Israel's true heirs; "Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans" (John 4:9). A Samaritan village had refused Jesus (9:52–53). Yet the Samaritan is the hero of the parable of the neighbor (10:33) and here the only one of ten who gives thanks. The scene recalls Naaman, the foreign general healed of skin disease, who "returned to the man of God with his whole troop" to give thanks (2 Kings 5:15), and whom Jesus had named in his first sermon (4:27). Luke prepares for the mission to Samaria in Acts 8.

t: The word on the temple wall
p: Ἀλλογενής, "foreigner", is the word on the temple inscription that barred non-Jews from the inner courts on pain of death.
b: Ἀλλογενής, "of another race," appears only here in the New Testament. It is the word carved on the stone notices in Herod's temple that warned any "foreigner" not to pass the barrier into the inner courts, on pain of death (Josephus, Jewish War 5.193–194; Antiquities 15.417). One of these inscriptions was found in Jerusalem in 1871. The man the temple shut out is the one who comes back to give glory to God and thanks to Jesus. In the Septuagint the word is used for the outsider (zar) who may not eat holy things (Leviticus 22:10).

p: All ten were cleansed. To the one who returned Jesus says, "Your faith has saved you".
b: Luke uses three verbs: the ten "were made clean" (17:14, 17), the Samaritan "saw that he had been healed" (17:15), and Jesus tells him, "Your faith has saved you" (σέσωκεν). Σῴζω means both "heal" and "save"; this site keeps "save" so the link stays visible (compare 7:50; 8:48; 18:42). Many readers think the word here means more than the cure all ten received: a restored relation with God, marked by faith and thanks. Others note that Luke uses the same words for healings without that extra sense (8:48).

a: so that people can watch closely for it
p: Παρατήρησις means close observation, as of omens or the stars. The Pharisees had been "watching" Jesus (14:1).
b: The noun παρατήρησις, used only here in the New Testament, means careful watching, the kind of observation astronomers and readers of omens practiced. Many Jews of the time looked for signs and calculations that would show when God's kingdom would come (Daniel 9:24–27; 12:11–12). Jesus says the kingdom does not come on a schedule that can be tracked. There is irony too: the related verb described the Pharisees "keeping a close eye" on Jesus himself (14:1; 6:7; 20:20). They are watching him for faults, and missing the kingdom in front of them.

a: the kingdom of God is among you
p: Ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can mean "within you" (KJV) or "among you, in your midst". Each has a long history.
b: Three main readings. (1) "Within you": the KJV and many church fathers took it as an inner, spiritual kingdom in the heart (Origen, On Prayer 25); Tolstoy made it the title of his book on nonviolence (1894); the Gospel of Thomas says the kingdom "is inside you and outside you" (Thomas 3). Against this, Jesus is speaking to Pharisees, and Luke never calls the kingdom an inner state. (2) "Among you, in your midst": the kingdom is already present in Jesus and his deeds (11:20). Most modern translations take this view. (3) "Within your reach": C. H. Roberts argued from Greek papyri that ἐντός could mean "in your power." A fourth view hears a future: the kingdom will suddenly be among you, like lightning (17:24).
orig: ἐντὸς ὑμῶν (entos hymōn), 'within you, among you'

a: one of the days of the Son of Man
p: After Jesus is gone, the disciples will long for even one day of his presence or his coming.
b: Jesus now turns from the Pharisees to the disciples, and from the present kingdom to the future. "The days of the Son of Man" are like "the days of Noah" and "the days of Lot" (17:26–28). The phrase may mean the days of his earthly ministry, which the disciples will miss after he is gone (5:35), or the days of his coming in glory, which they will long for in hard times. Luke's readers, waiting under pressure for Jesus' return, would hear both. Compare the cry of the martyrs, "How long?" (Revelation 6:10).

p: Matthew and Mark place the same warning in the discourse on the Mount of Olives.
b: Matthew and Mark warn that people will say, "See, the Messiah is here!" and that false messiahs will rise (Matthew 24:23–26; Mark 13:21–22). Luke has a separate speech about the end in 21:5–36 and gives this material here, on the road to Jerusalem. The Jewish War of AD 66–70 brought several men who claimed to be deliverers, and Josephus describes prophets who led crowds into the wilderness (Jewish War 2.258–263). Jesus' word is simple: do not chase rumors.

p: The Son of Man's coming will be sudden and seen by all, not a rumor in a back room.
b: Lightning lights the whole sky at once, "from one side under the sky to the other side." No one needs to be told where it is. Matthew has the same image, east to west (Matthew 24:27). The point answers 17:23: when the Son of Man comes, no one will need a report. Daniel's vision of "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven stands behind all these sayings (Daniel 7:13–14).

a: be thrown out by this generation
p: Luke sets a prediction of the Passion right in the middle of the sayings about the end.
b: Before the glory, suffering: Jesus repeats his prediction of 9:22 (Mark 8:31), and the verb ἀποδοκιμάζω, "reject, throw out," is the one in Psalm 118: "A stone that the builders threw out" (Psalm 118:22; compare Luke 20:17). Only Luke places a Passion saying here, among the sayings about the day of the Son of Man. It is a key to the whole Gospel: the risen Jesus asks whether the Messiah did not have to suffer before entering his glory (24:26). "This generation" are Jesus' contemporaries who reject him (7:31; 11:29–32).

p: Jewish writers paired Noah and Lot as people rescued from judgment. So does 2 Peter.
b: Matthew uses Noah's flood alone (Matthew 24:37–39); Luke adds Lot and Sodom (17:28–29). The pair was a familiar one: the Wisdom of Solomon speaks of the flood and of Lot rescued from the fire that fell on the five cities (Wisdom of Solomon 10:4–7), and 2 Peter sets Noah and Lot side by side as righteous people God rescued while he judged the ungodly (2 Peter 2:5–9). The sin Jesus names is not gross wickedness but ordinary life lived as if God would never act: eating, drinking, marrying, trading, building.
r: Genesis 6:5–7:23; Matthew 24:37–39; Wisdom of Solomon 10:4–7; 2 Peter 2:5–9; Hebrews 11:7

a: they ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built
p: The six verbs, with no "and" between them, picture a busy, prosperous city that did not see judgment coming.
b: Luke strings six verbs together with no "and" between them, a rushing picture of a city at work and at table. Genesis says Sodom's sin was "very grave" (Genesis 18:20), and Ezekiel names its pride, its plenty and its neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus' list is deliberately ordinary: the danger is not some exotic vice, but a life so full of buying and building that it has no room for God. Compare the rich fool, who planned to build bigger barns (12:16–21), and the excuses of 14:18–20.

a: it rained fire and sulfur from heaven
p: Luke's words follow the Greek of Genesis 19:24.
b: The words follow the Septuagint of Genesis 19:24: "Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD, out of the sky" (Genesis 19:24). Luke leaves the subject unnamed, "it rained," but every hearer knew who sent it. Sulfur (θεῖον, KJV "brimstone") became a fixed part of the picture of judgment (Psalm 11:6; Ezekiel 38:22; Revelation 14:10; 19:20). Note the timing: judgment fell "on the day Lot went out," once the righteous were safely away.
r: Genesis 19:24; Psalm 11:6; Ezekiel 38:22; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 19:20; 2 Peter 2:6–7

a: the Son of Man is unveiled
p: The verb is ἀποκαλύπτω, "reveal", from which comes "apocalypse".
b: Ἀποκαλύπτεται means "is uncovered, revealed." The Son of Man is not created on that day; he is shown for who he already is. Paul and 1 Peter use the noun ἀποκάλυψις for the same event: believers wait for "the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:7; 2 Thessalonians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:7, 13). The last book of the Bible takes its name, the Apocalypse, from the same word (Revelation 1:1).

a: whoever is up on the roof
p: In Mark and Matthew this warning is about fleeing Jerusalem. In Luke it is about not clinging to possessions on the last day.
b: Mark and Matthew put the warning about the roof and the field in the discourse on the Mount of Olives, where it tells people in Judea to flee at once when the city is threatened (Mark 13:14–16; Matthew 24:16–18). Luke has his own version of that warning about Jerusalem in 21:21. Here he uses the roof and the field for the day of the Son of Man, and adds, "Remember Lot's wife!" Fleeing makes little sense at the coming of the Son of Man, so Luke's point is different: on that day, do not turn back for your belongings. Flat roofs were used for work and rest, and an outside stair let a person come down without going into the house.

p: She looked back toward Sodom and became a pillar of salt. The shortest saying in Luke.
b: "His wife, coming behind him, looked back, and she turned into a pillar of salt" (Genesis 19:26). Jewish writers made her a warning: the Wisdom of Solomon speaks of the pillar of salt standing as a monument to an unbelieving soul (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7), and Josephus says he had seen the pillar himself (Antiquities 1.203). She had left Sodom, but her heart had not. Jesus has already said that no one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom (9:62).

p: Luke's verb was used of the Hebrew midwives who "kept the boys alive" in Egypt.
b: The saying about losing and saving one's life appears six times in the Gospels (9:24; Matthew 10:39; Matthew 16:25; Mark 8:35; John 12:25), each time in slightly different words. Luke's form here has two rare verbs. Περιποιέομαι means "keep safe, acquire"; ζῳογονέω means "preserve alive," the word the Septuagint uses for the Hebrew midwives who "kept the boys alive" (Exodus 1:17) and that Stephen uses of Pharaoh's attempt to keep Hebrew babies from living (Acts 7:19). Whoever clutches at life loses it; whoever lets it go is kept alive by God.
r: 9:24; Matthew 10:39; Matthew 16:25; Mark 8:35; John 12:25; Exodus 1:17; Acts 7:19

a: One will be taken along, and the other will be left behind
t: Taken or left: which is better?
p: Some read the "taken" as rescued (the rapture); others as swept away in judgment, as by the flood.
b: Παραλαμβάνω means "take along, take to oneself"; Jesus uses it of taking his disciples to be with him (John 14:3). Many readers, especially Dispensationalists, take the ones "taken along" as believers gathered to Christ, and some as the rapture before a time of tribulation. Others note that in the stories just told, Noah and Lot were taken out of danger, while those left behind were destroyed, which supports the same reading; still others think the flood that "carried them all off" (Matthew 24:39) points the other way, so that the ones taken are taken in judgment. Luke's own question in 17:37 ("Where, Lord?") is answered with vultures, suggesting judgment. See the card at Matthew 24:40.

p: Grinding grain was women's work, done at dawn with two women at one hand mill.
b: Every household ground its grain daily on a hand mill, often two women working together, one feeding the grain and the other turning the upper stone, before dawn (compare Exodus 11:5; Jeremiah 25:10). Luke pairs a night scene (two in one bed) with a morning one (two at the mill), which suggests that the day of the Son of Man will come everywhere at once, whatever the hour where people are.

p: Ἀετοί usually means eagles, but birds that gather at a dead body are vultures. The saying is a proverb.
b: Ἀετός is the usual Greek for "eagle," but ancient writers did not separate eagles and vultures as carefully as modern bird books do, and the birds that gather at a dead body are vultures (Job 39:30: "wherever there are bodies, it is there"; Habakkuk 1:8). The disciples ask "Where?", and Jesus answers with a proverb, not a map: as surely as circling birds show where a carcass lies, judgment will be plain to see wherever it falls. Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 24:28), with πτῶμα, "corpse"; Luke has σῶμα, "body." Some interpreters, reading the passage of AD 70, think of the eagles on the standards of the Roman legions.
